drills.q: What is a Unix debugger built out of?
options: One system call, multiplexed over a dozen requests, plus bookkeeping in userspace
A kernel debugging subsystem the debugger attaches to
A library the traced program has to be linked against
A virtual machine the program runs inside
drills.why: There is no debugger subsystem. Read and write memory, read and write registers, resume, single step, and wait: everything else is built from those.

drills.q: How is a breakpoint installed on x86?
options: The first byte at the address is replaced with a one byte trap instruction
The address is written to a kernel table of breakpoints
The page is marked non-executable so access faults
The instruction is replaced with a jump to the debugger
drills.why: The trap byte's entire purpose is to raise a debug trap. Installing a breakpoint is a read of one word and a write of one word.

drills.q: Where is the instruction pointer when a breakpoint trap is taken?
options: One past the breakpoint, because the trap byte was executed and consumed
At the breakpoint address
At the start of the next instruction after the original one
Wherever the previous jump left it
drills.why: The debugger has to read the registers, subtract one and write them back. Without that the program resumes into the middle of an instruction.

drills.q: What does resuming from an armed breakpoint require?
options: Restore the original byte, single step one instruction, write the trap byte again, continue
Continue, since the trap has already been consumed
Remove the breakpoint and reinstall it at the next hit
Rewrite the whole page and flush the instruction cache
drills.why: That dance is several system calls and two context switches on every hit, which is why a breakpoint in a hot loop feels like a hang.

drills.q: Why is timing a program under a debugger meaningless?
options: Breakpoints modify the program's instructions and every hit costs system calls and context switches
The debugger runs the program at a lower priority
Debug information makes the binary larger and slower
The kernel disables the cache while a process is traced
drills.why: It also means anything that checksums its own code notices that its text has changed.

drills.q: How many hardware watchpoints does x86-64 have, and how wide is each?
options: Four, each covering at most eight bytes
Eight, each covering one page
One per general purpose register
As many as memory allows; they are a kernel structure
drills.why: Small, fixed, and worth remembering, because exceeding it does not produce an error.

drills.q: What happens when you ask to watch something that does not fit in the debug registers?
options: The debugger silently falls back to single stepping the whole program and re-checking after every instruction
It reports that no watchpoint registers are available
It watches the first eight bytes and ignores the rest
It sets a breakpoint on every function that could write to it
drills.why: The manual describes the fallback as hundreds of times slower than normal execution. Someone who does not know about it concludes the debugger has hung.

drills.q: Why is optimised code harder to debug?
options: The question becomes ambiguous: a variable may be in a register with no address, an inlined function has no frame, and one instruction can belong to two lines
The compiler stops emitting debug information above -O0
Optimised code cannot have breakpoints installed in it
The debug tables are compressed and only partly readable
drills.why: The tables are telling the truth about a program whose shape no longer matches the source you are reading.

options: A compiler pass that rewrites the program to check itself, plus a runtime that keeps the metadata
A library that replaces the allocator at load time
A separate process that watches the program's memory
A static analysis run before compilation
drills.why: That is why it needs a recompile, why uninstrumented code is invisible to it, and why it is far faster than a tool working from the binary alone.

drills.q: What is the address sanitizer's shadow mapping?
options: Eight application bytes map to one shadow byte, found by shifting right three and adding an offset
Each byte has a shadow byte, in a parallel region
Each allocation has a header describing its state
Each page has a descriptor in a side table
drills.why: A shift and an add, which is why the check in front of every load and store is cheap enough to leave on.

drills.q: A shadow byte holds the value 4. What does that mean?
options: The first four of those eight bytes are addressable and the last four are not
Four of the eight are poisoned, in unspecified positions
The block was freed four allocations ago
Four bytes of redzone follow
drills.why: The partial case works only because allocations are eight byte aligned, so a block can be partial at its end and never at its start.

drills.q: What does a negative shadow byte encode?
options: All eight bytes are poisoned, and the value says why: a redzone, freed memory, use after return, and so on
The number of bytes that overflowed
A pointer into the allocator's metadata
That the region has never been touched
drills.why: Those values are what the legend in a sanitizer report is decoding for you.

options: Padding around every allocation, poisoned, so a small overflow lands somewhere already marked bad
Extra space so the allocator can grow a block in place
Memory reserved for the sanitizer's own bookkeeping
A region where allocations are deliberately slow, to expose races
drills.why: Without it, an overflow of one element lands in the next object, where it is silent and corrupts real data.

drills.q: How does the address sanitizer catch use after free at all?
options: Freed blocks are poisoned and held on a queue instead of being reused immediately
Every pointer is checked against a table of live allocations
Freed pages are unmapped, so any access faults
The compiler proves that no pointer outlives its allocation
drills.why: Not reusing the address is what keeps the shadow byte saying freed rather than describing whatever was allocated there next.

drills.q: What does a clean address sanitizer run prove?
options: That no violation happened inside the detection window, on the paths this run took, in code that was recompiled
That the program has no memory errors
That the program has no use after free, though it may have overflows
Nothing at all, since the instrumentation changes the program
drills.why: The quarantine gives a window measured in allocation traffic. Beyond it the address is handed out again and the bug is silent, so this is a detector rather than a proof.
